newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SNB price surge leaves officials bemused.
newsitem.headline: SNB price surge leaves officials bemused.

text.p: The Swiss National Bank (SNB), Switzerland's central bank, is not your average stock company, but its shares lately have been moving sharply higher, much to the bemusement of SNB officials and financial analysts.

Small investors are believed behind the rise in its share price which began in early March when the Swiss government announced it would create a humanitarian fund based on money gained from a proposed revaluation of the SNB's gold reserves.
Credit Suisse analyst Stefan Buchli called the latest share price rise "astonishing."
"After these shares have practically not moved for years, in the last two trading days they have risen by over 40 percent," Buchli said.
The SNB's share price, which in early March was just over 600 Swiss francs ($417), was quoted on Thursday as high as 1,200 francs.
On Wednesday its stock closed at 1,100 francs after setting a year high of 1,330 francs on volume of 2,849 shares.

The SNB, in what analysts say is an unusual structure for a central bank, has 35,084 shares in public hands, out of a total of 100,000 shares. Most of the rest -- 63 percent -- are held by Swiss cantons, cantonal banks and other public institutions.
It holds an annual shareholders' meeting which is well-attended, and domestic shareholders have voting rights.
In addition, 451 of its shares were held by foreigners at the end of 1996, its annual report said.
The SNB, as public institutions go, has its strengths, including a 90-year tradition and a monopoly on printing money.

It set higher returns in 1996, thanks in part to the Swiss franc's declines which boosted the value of foreign currency reserves, held mainly in dollars. Most returns are paid out to the government or kept as provisions. It is expected to see some revenue enhancements, providing Swiss constitutional changes are approved.

It has lately come under fire, along with the rest of the Swiss financial community, for its role in World War Two, and it has faced criticism that it bought gold from the Nazis, although the humanitarian fund proposed by the Swiss government has mitigated the criticism somewhat.
The changes required for the fund are alongside plans to allow the SNB to be more flexible in managing its assets.
A partial revision of its laws, if approved, would allow it to participate in gold lending, for example, and give it more freedom in terms of the maturities of its investments.
According to the SNB's annual report, the partial revision of its law should, on average, lead to a surplus income of around 400 million francs annually.
Under its chairman Hans Meyer, who took over last year, the SNS also has introduced changes.

For example, its annual report for 1996 was restyled, and now resembles more those of private-sector banks. It also changed the format for its 10-day reserve statements this year to allow greater transparency.
But the SNB is also highly unlikely to make any private shareholders rich.
Buchli, who believes the buying is being done by small investors, added they were likely misguided if they were purchasing SNB shares based on expectations of a higher payout.
The SNB has its dividend legally mandated, and it does not appear to be planning changes in its dividend policy.
SNB officials viewed the latest share gains with a mixture of surprise and good humour.
"It is really an odd subject for a central bank to become a high flyer at the stock exchange. We hope it is because of the quality of monetary policy," said SNB spokesman Werner Abegg,
Abegg said that the matter of the shareholder value, which has become a buzzword in Switzerland lately, was not to be taken lightly, but added:
"We have other tasks -- monetary and foreign exchange policy -- I would say the best shareholder value we can offer is a good monetary policy."
-- Zurich Editorial, +41 1 631 7340
($ = 1.438 Swiss Francs)
